posts.title: Flu and COVID vaccination clinics open on 2 November
posts.excerpt: Our autumn vaccination clinics start on Monday 2 November. Booking opens today, by phone from 07:30 or online.
posts.content:
Our autumn flu and COVID vaccination clinics begin on Monday 2 November. Each clinic is run by the nurses in the treatment room, and Ruth Okafor will be in charge of the schedule. Booking opens today, by phone from 07:30 or online at any time.

The clinics run on Monday and Wednesday afternoons from 14:00 to 18:00, and on Saturday mornings from 08:30 to 12:00 with Dr Lindqvist. The last clinic of the season is on Saturday 12 December. You do not need to be seen by a doctor first: the nurse will check your record and confirm that the vaccination is right for you.

Flu vaccination is offered to people aged 65 and over, to adults and children with certain long-term conditions, to pregnant women, and to some carers. COVID vaccination follows the national invitation list. If you are not sure whether you are on a list, ring reception and we will look at your record while you wait on the line.

Each visit takes about ten minutes. Please wear a top with sleeves that roll up above the elbow, and bring your invitation letter if you have one. If you have had a reaction to a vaccine before, or you feel unwell with a high temperature on the day, tell the nurse or ring us to move the appointment.

You are welcome to bring a family member. If you want both vaccinations, we can usually give them at the same visit, and the nurse will explain which arm to use and what you may notice afterwards. A sore arm for a day or two is common, and the nurse will tell you what to do if you feel unwell.

If you cannot come to the clinic, tell reception when you book. Patients who cannot travel can be vaccinated on the Thursday home-visit afternoon, but these slots are limited, so please ask early. Everyone who is vaccinated at Linden Row has the date recorded in their notes, so you can always ask us what you have had and when.

Booking line: 01632 960 418, from 07:30 on weekdays. Online booking is on the Vaccinations and checks page.

posts.title: What to bring to your first appointment
posts.excerpt: A short list of what helps us in the first ten minutes, and what you can leave at home.
posts.content:
If you are joining Sukoyaka Family Clinic, your first appointment is mostly about getting to know you. It is usually twenty minutes long, with a nurse or a doctor, and it helps if you bring a few things with you. None of them is essential, and we will work with whatever you have.

Please bring something that shows your name and address, such as a letter or a utility bill, and your registration form if you filled it in at home. If you have an insurance or health card, bring that too. Reception will check the details when you arrive, which takes about five minutes, so please come a little early.

The most useful thing is a list of your medicines. A photograph of the box or the repeat slip is fine. Include things you buy yourself, such as vitamins, creams or herbal remedies, because they can matter when we choose a treatment. If you take medicines at particular times, write that down as well.

Bring any recent letters from hospitals or specialists, and the dates of operations or vaccinations if you remember them. If your previous practice has sent your records, we will already have much of this, but a short summary in your own words is still helpful.

It also helps to write down your questions beforehand. Many people forget half of them once they are in the room. Put the most important one first, so that we deal with it before the time runs out. If you have several problems, tell reception when you book and we will give you twenty minutes.

If you would like someone with you, a relative or friend is welcome. If you need an interpreter or a female doctor or nurse, ask when you book and we will arrange it. For children, bring the baby book or vaccination card if you have one.

You can leave at home: your old prescriptions, the box of every tablet you have ever taken, and any worry about asking a question that sounds silly. Reception is open from 08:00 to 18:00, and the phone line from 07:30.

posts.title: Blood tests: why we ask you to come before ten
posts.excerpt: The treatment room takes blood tests until 10:00. Here is the reason, and what happens to the sample afterwards.
posts.content:
If you have been asked to have a blood test, we will usually ask you to come between 08:00 and 10:00. There is a practical reason, and it is worth knowing so that you can plan your morning.

The courier collects the samples from Linden Row at midday and takes them to the laboratory. Most blood samples need to be handled within a few hours of being taken, so a sample taken at 09:50 can be packed and ready, while one taken at 11:30 would wait until the next day. A sample that waits is more likely to need repeating.

Some tests need you not to have eaten or drunk anything but water for eight to twelve hours beforehand. A morning appointment makes that easier, because most of the fasting happens while you sleep. When you book, reception will tell you whether your test needs fasting. Please take your usual medicines with water unless the doctor has said otherwise.

On the day, check in at reception and take a seat. The treatment room opens at 08:00. A nurse calls you in, confirms your name and date of birth, and takes the sample. The visit usually takes about five minutes. If you do not like needles, tell the nurse before you start; you can lie down, and we can take a little longer.

After the sample leaves at midday, the laboratory runs the tests. Most routine results come back to the doctor within two to five working days. Some tests take longer, and we will say so when you have the blood taken. The doctor reads the result and either rings you or asks you to come in for a follow-up appointment.

If you cannot come before ten, ring reception. A few tests, such as those for certain hormones, must be taken at a particular time, and we will explain if that applies to you. For children, the nurse may use a numbing cream, which takes about forty-five minutes to work, so ask when you book.

If you have not heard anything after a week, please ring and ask for the nurse's desk. Not hearing from us is not a result, and we would rather check than leave you wondering.

posts.title: Living with high blood pressure: a review every six months
posts.excerpt: How the six-monthly blood-pressure review works at Linden Row, and how you can prepare for it.
posts.content:
Many of our patients live with high blood pressure, and we see them for a review every six months. The review is a twenty-minute visit with the nurse and, when needed, with Dr Hart, who has a special interest in long-term conditions.

The visit follows a fixed order, so that you know what to expect. First the nurse measures your blood pressure, sitting down after five minutes of rest, and measures it again if the first reading is higher than usual. She also weighs you and asks about your medicines, and whether you have any side effects. Then she writes the numbers on a card for you to keep.

If you have a home blood-pressure monitor, bring it to the first review so that the nurse can check it against ours. Readings taken at home are useful because many people feel tense in a clinic. Write down your readings for a week before the visit, morning and evening, and bring the list. Seven days of numbers tells us more than one reading on the day.

We usually ask for a blood test and a urine sample once a year, to look at how the kidneys are working and at cholesterol. The blood test can be done before the review, in the treatment room before 10:00, so that the results are ready when you come in.

The doctor looks at the numbers with you and decides whether anything should change. Sometimes nothing does, and we simply book the next review. If a change is suggested, such as a different dose, the doctor explains why and writes down what to do and when to come back. We do not change treatment without telling you.

There are things that do not need an appointment. If you feel dizzy, or have a new headache that will not go away, or your home readings are much higher than usual on several days, ring the surgery and ask for a nurse or doctor to call you back. In an emergency, call 999.

Your next review date is booked before you leave, and reception sends a reminder text a week before. If you cannot come, please ring to move it rather than let it lapse.

posts.title: The first year: our baby check timetable
posts.excerpt: The visits we offer in a baby's first year, who does them and what happens at each one.
posts.content:
A baby's first year has a rhythm of checks and vaccinations. This is our timetable at Linden Row, so that you know what is coming and can plan around it. Each visit is booked for twenty minutes, in the children's room on the ground floor.

The first check is in the first two weeks, usually with Dr Lindqvist or Dr Hart. They listen to the heart and lungs, look at the hips, eyes and skin, check feeding and ask how you are. We also register your baby with the clinic at this visit and give you the baby book if you do not already have one.

At about six to eight weeks there is a second check with the doctor, together with the first vaccination appointment with a nurse. The nurse explains each vaccination before giving it, writes it in the baby book and tells you what to expect afterwards. Further vaccination visits follow at about twelve and sixteen weeks, and again around the first birthday.

Between the doctor's checks, the nurses weigh and measure your baby whenever you like. You do not need an appointment for a weight check on Thursdays between 14:00 and 16:00, though you may wait for a few minutes. The growth chart in the baby book shows how your baby is growing over time, and the nurse will go through it with you.

At about nine to twelve months we ask you to come for a development check. The nurse looks at how your baby sits, crawls, babbles and plays, and answers questions about sleep, feeding and starting solid food. If anything needs a closer look, she will explain it and arrange it.

We set aside same-day appointments each morning for babies and children who are unwell. If your baby has a high temperature, is feeding poorly or you are worried, ring from 07:30 and say how old your baby is. For anything that seems very serious, call 999.

Bring the baby book to every visit. If you are not sure when the next one is due, ring reception and ask for a nurse. We will look at your baby's record and tell you which appointment comes next.

posts.title: Thursday home visits: how they work
posts.excerpt: Dr Hart visits patients who cannot easily come to the clinic on Thursday afternoons. Here is how to ask for a visit.
posts.content:
On Thursday afternoons, Dr Ellen Hart visits patients at home. It is a part of the clinic's week that she has kept since the early years, and she still does the visits herself. Here is how they work, for patients and for the people who care for them.

Home visits are for people who cannot reasonably come to the clinic: for example, because they are frail, housebound or very unwell. They are not for people who find it inconvenient to travel. If you are not sure, ring reception and tell us what is happening; we will decide together with you.

To ask for a visit, ring the booking line from 07:30 on Monday to Thursday morning. Reception will ask a few questions: what the problem is, how long it has lasted, whether the patient has a carer, and the address. A doctor reads the answers and may ring you back before deciding whether a visit is the right step.

On Thursday morning, Grace Whitfield's team gives each person a time window, and Ruth Okafor or one of the nurses rings the day before to confirm. Visits usually take twenty to thirty minutes. Dr Hart brings a bag with a blood-pressure monitor, tests for common infections and the equipment for taking blood.

If a blood test is needed, she takes it at the visit and brings it back to Linden Row for the midday courier on Friday. Prescriptions are sent to the dispensary, and the dispensary arranges delivery if there is nobody to collect them. Notes from the visit are written into the record the same day.

If a patient needs help urgently on another day, ring the surgery as usual, or the on-call service out of hours. A home visit on a Thursday is not a substitute for urgent care. For an emergency, call 999.

Carers are welcome to be present, and we often ask them to be, because they know the patient best. If you look after someone who receives visits, tell reception, and we can give you a named contact for questions between visits.
